report:
## Conclusion

The claim that soursop "cures cancer" in humans is **false**, or at least unsupported by reliable evidence. Your skepticism is well-founded.

## What the evidence shows

**Lab studies vs. human evidence:** Soursop (also called graviola or guanabana) contains bioactive compounds called acetogenins that have shown anti-proliferative effects on cancer cells *in vitro* (in petri dishes) and in some animal models. However, no controlled clinical trials in humans have demonstrated that soursop cures or effectively treats cancer. As PolitiFact notes, "there haven't been human studies, so we don't know whether it can work as a cancer treatment or not" (https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/).

**Major medical institutions agree:** According to Wikipedia's summary of positions from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Cancer Research UK, cancer treatment using soursop "is not supported by reliable clinical evidence," and internet claims promoting graviola capsules as a cancer cure lack scientific backing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop). Fact-checkers at Snopes similarly found that while lab research shows "potential anticancer properties," no evidence supports its use as an actual cancer "cure" (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/).

**Safety concerns:** Beyond lacking proven efficacy, soursop consumption carries documented health risks. Research has linked long-term, heavy consumption of Annonaceae fruits (including soursop) to atypical parkinsonism, likely due to neurotoxic acetogenins like annonacin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annonacin).

## Bottom line

The scientific consensus is that soursop shows preliminary, lab-based anticancer activity but has not been proven safe or effective as a cancer treatment in humans. Claims that it "cures cancer" are unsupported and potentially dangerous if they discourage people from pursuing evidence-based treatment.
